events.label: Holmes describes Porlock and Moriarty to Watson

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: Porlock is a nom-de-plume, a mere identification mark; behind it lies a shifty and evasive personality. In a former letter he informed me that the name was not his own. Porlock is important for the great man with whom he is in touch. You have heard me speak of Professor Moriarty?

events.label: Watson refers to Moriarty as a famous scientific criminal and unknown to the public

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: The famous scientific criminal, as famous among crooks as... unknown to the public.

events.label: Holmes praises Watson's humor and extols Moriarty

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: My blushes, Watson! A touch! A distinct touch! You are developing a certain unexpected vein of pawky humour, Watson, against which I must learn to guard myself. But in calling Moriarty a criminal you are uttering libel in the eyes of the law—and there lie the glory and the wonder of it! The greatest schemer of all time, the organizer of every deviltry, the controlling brain of the underworld, a brain which might have made or marred the destiny of nations—that’s the man! But so aloof is he from general suspicion, so immune from criticism, so admirable in his management and self-effacement, that for those very words that you have uttered he could hale you to a court and emerge with your year’s pension as a solatium for his wounded character. Is he not the celebrated author of The Dynamics of an Asteroid, a book which ascends to such rarefied heights of pure mathematics that it is said that there was no man in the scientific press capable of criticizing it? Is this a man to traduce? Foul-mouthed doctor and slandered professor—such would be your respective rôles! That’s genius, Watson. But if I am spared by lesser men, our day will surely come.

events.label: Watson expresses a wish to be present for that day

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: May I be there to see!

events.label: Holmes says Porlock is a link in the chain and the only flaw so far

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: Ah, yes—the so-called Porlock is a link in the chain some little way from its great attachment. Porlock is not quite a sound link—between ourselves. He is the only flaw in that chain so far as I have been able to test it.

events.label: Holmes explains the importance of Porlock

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: Hence the extreme importance of Porlock. He has once or twice given me advance information which has been of value. If we had the cipher, we should find that this communication is of the nature that I indicate.

events.label: Holmes examines the paper and Watson looks at the inscription
Holmes identifies the inscription as secret information

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: It is obviously an attempt to convey secret information. In this instance, the cipher has no use at all. The message is a reference to the words in a page of some book, and I am powerless until I am told which page and which book. Douglas and Birlstone are words not contained in the page in question. One should not include cipher and message in the same envelope because if it miscarried one would be undone. Our second post is overdue, and I shall be surprised if it does not bring us either a further letter of explanation or the volume to which these figures refer.

events.label: Billy delivers the expected letter
Holmes opens and reads the letter
Holmes considers the letter and mentions Moriarty

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: After all, there may be nothing in it. It may be only his guilty conscience. Knowing himself to be a traitor, he may have read the accusation in the other’s eyes. The other being, I presume, Professor Moriarty. No less. When any of that party talk about 'He' you know whom they mean. There is one predominant 'He' for all of them.

events.label: The speakers discuss the cipher and infer properties of the referenced book

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: Let us consider the problem in the light of pure reason. This man’s reference is to a book. That is our point of departure. We may take it as a working hypothesis that 534 is the particular page to which the cipher refers. The book is a very common book. The book is standardized, and page 534 in his copy will exactly agree with my page 534.

events.label: Watson identifies the Bible as the book and Holmes rejects it as the match

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: The Bible!

events.label: Holmes and Watson reject Bradshaw and the dictionary as possible message sources

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: There are difficulties, Watson. The vocabulary of Bradshaw is nervous and terse, but limited. The selection of words would hardly lend itself to the sending of general messages. We will eliminate Bradshaw. The dictionary is, I fear, inadmissible for the same reason. What then is left?

events.label: Watson proposes an almanac as the source

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: An almanac!

events.label: Holmes examines Whitaker's Almanac and begins decoding the message

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: Excellent, Watson! I am very much mistaken if you have not touched the spot. An almanac! Let us consider the claims of Whitaker’s Almanac. It is in common use. It has the requisite number of pages. It is in double column. Though reserved in its earlier vocabulary, it becomes, if I remember right, quite garrulous towards the end. Here is page 534, column two, a substantial block of print dealing, I perceive, with the trade and resources of British India. Jot down the words, Watson! Number thirteen is ‘Mahratta.’ Not, I fear, a very auspicious beginning. Number one hundred and twenty-seven is ‘Government’; which at least makes sense, though somewhat irrelevant to ourselves and Professor Moriarty. Now let us try again. What does the Mahratta government do? Alas! the next word is ‘pig’s-bristles.’ We are undone, my good Watson! It is finished!

events.label: Holmes fetches a second yellow-covered volume from a cupboard
Holmes explains that they may be using the new almanac instead of the old one

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: We pay the price, Watson, for being too up-to-date! We are before our time, and suffer the usual penalties. Being the seventh of January, we have very properly laid in the new almanac. It is more than likely that Porlock took his message from the old one. No doubt he would have told us so had his letter of explanation been written.

events.label: Holmes deciphers the message in the old almanac

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: Now let us see what page 534 has in store for us. Number thirteen is ‘There,’ which is much more promising. Number one hundred and twenty-seven is ‘is’—‘There is’ ‘danger.’ Ha! Ha! Capital! Put that down, Watson. ‘There is danger—may—come—very soon—one.’ Then we have the name ‘Douglas’—‘rich—country—now—at Birlstone—House—Birlstone—confidence—is—pressing.’ There, Watson! What do you think of pure reason and its fruit? If the green-grocer had such a thing as a laurel wreath, I should send Billy round for it. ... The purport is perfectly clear. Some deviltry is intended against one Douglas, whoever he may be, residing as stated, a rich country gentleman. He is sure—‘confidence’ was as near as he could get to ‘confident’—that it is pressing. There is our result—and a very workmanlike little bit of analysis it was!

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: That painting was by Jean Baptiste Greuze. Jean Baptiste Greuze was a French artist who flourished between the years 1750 and 1800. I allude, of course to his working career. Modern criticism has more than indorsed the high opinion formed of him by his contemporaries.

events.label: Holmes explains that all knowledge is useful to the detective

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: All knowledge comes useful to the detective. Even the trivial fact that in the year 1865 a picture by Greuze entitled ‘La Jeune Fille à l’Agneau’ fetched one million two hundred thousand francs—more than forty thousand pounds—at the Portalis sale may start a train of reflection in your mind.

communicates.speaker: holmes

events.label: Holmes says he examined Moriarty’s rooms three times

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: I have been three times in his rooms, twice waiting for him under different pretexts and leaving before he came. Once—well, I can hardly tell about the once to an official detective. It was on the last occasion that I took the liberty of running over his papers—with the most unexpected results.

communicates.speaker: holmes

events.label: Holmes infers illegal income from Moriarty’s wealth

communicates.speaker: holmes

Of course I have other reasons for thinking so—dozens of exiguous threads which lead vaguely up towards the centre of the web where the poisonous, motionless creature is lurking. I only mention the Greuze because it brings the matter within the range of your own observation.

communicates.content: Moriarty is the first link in his chain, with this Napoleon-gone-wrong at one end, and a hundred broken fighting men, pickpockets, blackmailers, and card sharpers at the other, with every sort of crime in between.

That you get from the warning received through the man Porlock. Can we for our present practical needs get any further than that?

events.label: Holmes proposes that Moriarty may have ordered a murder to enforce discipline or as ordinary business

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: We may form some conception as to the motives of the crime. There might be two different motives. Moriarty rules with a rod of iron over his people. His discipline is tremendous. There is only one punishment in his code. It is death. The murdered man Douglas may have betrayed the chief, and his punishment followed to put the fear of death into them. The other is that it has been engineered by Moriarty in the ordinary course of business. If there was robbery, it would be against the first hypothesis and in favour of the second. Moriarty may have been engaged to engineer it on a promise of part spoils, or he may have been paid so much down to manage it. Whichever it may be, it is down at Birlstone that we must seek the solution. I know our man too well to suppose that he has left anything up here which may lead us to him.

events.label: MacDonald urges the group to go to Birlstone

communicates.speaker: macdonald

events.label: MacDonald says he has five minutes for preparation

communicates.speaker: macdonald
communicates.content: it’s later than I thought. I can give you, gentlemen, five minutes for preparation, and that is all.

communicates.speaker: macdonald
communicates.content: All about it proved to be disappointingly little, and yet there was enough to assure us that the case before us might well be worthy of the expert’s closest attention.

events.label: MacDonald explains how he received the initial account and what it said

communicates.speaker: macdonald
communicates.content: That was in the inclosed official report. It didn’t say ‘horrible’: that’s not a recognized official term. It gave the name John Douglas. It mentioned that his injuries had been in the head, from the discharge of a shotgun. It also mentioned the hour of the alarm, which was close on to midnight last night. It added that the case was undoubtedly one of murder, but that no arrest had been made, and that the case was one which presented some very perplexing and extraordinary features. That’s absolutely all we have at present, Mr. Holmes.

events.label: Holmes declines to pursue premature theories and states the two known facts

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: Then, with your permission, we will leave it at that, Mr. Mac. The temptation to form premature theories upon insufficient data is the bane of our profession. I can see only two things for certain at present—a great brain in London, and a dead man in Sussex. It’s the chain between that we are going to trace.

communicates.content: It was just half-past eleven. I had not begun to undress, and I was sitting by the fire in my bedroom when I heard the report. It was not very loud—it seemed to be muffled. I rushed down—I don’t suppose it was thirty seconds before I was in the room.

events.label: Barker answers that the door was open

communicates.speaker: cecil_james_barker
communicates.content: Yes, it was open.

events.label: Barker describes Douglas lying in the room and the candle burning

communicates.speaker: cecil_james_barker
communicates.content: Poor Douglas was lying as you see him. His bedroom candle was burning on the table. It was I who lit the lamp some minutes afterward.

events.label: Barker says he saw no one and intercepted Mrs. Douglas

communicates.speaker: cecil_james_barker
communicates.content: No. I heard Mrs. Douglas coming down the stair behind me, and I rushed out to prevent her from seeing this dreadful sight. Mrs. Allen, the housekeeper, came and took her away. Ames had arrived, and we ran back into the room once more.

events.label: The sergeant asks about the drawbridge and Barker lowers it

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: I have heard that the drawbridge is kept up all night.

events.label: The sergeant suggests Douglas shot himself

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: Then how could any murderer have got away? It is out of the question! Mr. Douglas must have shot himself.

events.label: Barker shows the open window and blood mark
The sergeant and Barker discuss the moat escape

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: You mean that someone waded across the moat? Then if you were in the room within half a minute of the crime, he must have been in the water at that very moment.

events.label: The doctor comments on the injuries

communicates.speaker: dr_wood
communicates.content: Horrible enough! I’ve never seen such injuries since the Birlstone railway smash.

events.label: The sergeant questions how an outside person entered while the bridge was up

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: It’s all very well your saying that a man escaped by wading this moat, but what I ask you is, how did he ever get into the house at all if the bridge was up?

events.label: Ames answers when the bridge was raised

communicates.speaker: ames
communicates.content: It was nearly six o’clock. I’ve heard that it was usually raised at sunset. That would be nearer half-past four than six at this time of year. Mrs. Douglas had visitors to tea. I couldn’t raise it until they went. Then I wound it up myself.

events.label: The sergeant states how an outside killer must have entered and waited

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: If anyone came from outside—they must have got in across the bridge before six and been in hiding ever since, until Mr. Douglas came into the room after eleven. Mr. Douglas went round the house every night the last thing before he turned in to see that the lights were right. That brought him in here. The man was waiting and shot him. Then he got away through the window and left his gun behind him. That’s how I read it; for nothing else will fit the facts.

events.label: The sergeant picks up the card beside the dead man
The sergeant holds up the card and asks what it is

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: What's this?

events.label: Barker looks at the card with curiosity

communicates.speaker: cecil_james_barker
communicates.content: I never noticed it before.

communicates.speaker: cecil_james_barker
communicates.content: The murderer must have left it behind him.

events.label: The sergeant turns the card over in his fingers

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: What's V.V.? Somebody's initials, maybe.

events.label: The sergeant asks Dr. Wood what he has found

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: What have you got there, Dr. Wood?

events.label: The hammer is identified on the rug in front of the fireplace
Barker points to the box of nails on the mantelpiece

communicates.speaker: cecil_james_barker
communicates.content: Mr. Douglas was altering the pictures yesterday.

communicates.speaker: cecil_james_barker
communicates.content: I saw him myself, standing upon that chair and fixing the big picture above it. That accounts for the hammer.

events.label: The sergeant says the hammer should be put back on the rug

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: We'd best put it back on the rug where we found it.

events.label: The sergeant walks around the room with the lamp
The sergeant draws the window curtain aside and notices hiding signs
The sergeant asks when the curtains were drawn

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: What o'clock were those curtains drawn?

communicates.speaker: cecil_james_barker
communicates.content: When the lamps were lit. It would be shortly after four.

events.label: The sergeant states that someone had been hiding there

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: I’m bound to say this bears out your theory, Mr. Barker. It looks as if the man got into the house after four when the curtains were drawn, and before six when the bridge was raised. He slipped into this room, because it was the first that he saw. There was no other place where he could hide, so he popped in behind this curtain. That all seems clear enough. It is likely that his main idea was to burgle the house; but Mr. Douglas chanced to come upon him, so he murdered him and escaped.

events.label: Barker agrees with the sergeant's reading

communicates.speaker: cecil_james_barker
communicates.content: That's how I read it.

communicates.speaker: cecil_james_barker
communicates.content: But, I say, aren't we wasting precious time? Couldn't we start out and scout the country before the fellow gets away?

events.label: The sergeant says the suspect cannot get away by rail and should not be left yet

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: There are no trains before six in the morning; so he can't get away by rail. If he goes by road with his legs all dripping, it's odds that someone will notice him. Anyhow, I can't leave here myself until I am relieved. But I think none of you should go until we see more clearly how we all stand.

events.label: The doctor scrutinizes the body and notices a mark on the dead man's arm
The doctor says the mark is not tattooed and suggests the man was branded

communicates.speaker: dr_wood
communicates.content: It's not tattooed. I never saw anything like it. The man has been branded at some time as they brand cattle. What is the meaning of this?

events.label: Barker says he has seen the mark on Douglas many times for ten years

communicates.speaker: cecil_james_barker
communicates.content: I have seen the mark on Douglas many times this last ten years.

events.label: The butler says he has often noticed the same mark on Douglas

communicates.speaker: cecil_james_barker
communicates.content: And so have I. Many a time when the master has rolled up his sleeves I have noticed that very mark. I’ve often wondered what it could be.

events.label: The sergeant says the matter has nothing to do with the crime

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: Then it has nothing to do with the crime, anyhow

events.label: The butler exclaims and points at the dead man's outstretched hand
The butler reports that the dead man's wedding ring has been taken

communicates.speaker: mrs_allen
communicates.content: They’ve taken his wedding ring!

events.label: The butler explains the dead man's rings and identifies the missing wedding ring

communicates.speaker: mrs_allen
communicates.content: Master always wore his plain gold wedding ring on the little finger of his left hand. That ring with the rough nugget on it was above it, and the twisted snake ring on the third finger. There’s the nugget and there’s the snake, but the wedding ring is gone.

events.label: Barker confirms the butler's statement

communicates.speaker: cecil_james_barker
communicates.content: He’s right

events.label: The sergeant asks whether the wedding ring was below the other rings

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: Do you tell me that the wedding ring was below the other?

events.label: The butler answers that it was always below the other rings

communicates.speaker: mrs_allen
communicates.content: Always!

events.label: The sergeant describes how the murderer removed and replaced the rings

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: Then the murderer, or whoever it was, first took off this ring you call the nugget ring, then the wedding ring, and afterwards put the nugget ring back again.

events.label: The country policeman says London should be consulted on the case

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: Seems to me the sooner we get London on to this case the better. It won’t be long now before he is here to help us. But I expect we’ll have to look to London before we are through. Anyhow, I’m not ashamed to say that it is a deal too thick for the likes of me.

events.label: White Mason arrives from headquarters behind a trotter

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: his message

events.label: White Mason welcomes Holmes and Watson at Birlstone station
White Mason identifies the Westville Arms as the party's rooming place

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: Your room is at the Westville Arms. There’s no other place; but I hear that it is clean and good. The man will carry your bags. This way, gentlemen, if you please.

events.label: The group takes quarters at the inn
White Mason gives a rapid sketch of the previous events
MacDonald makes notes while Holmes listens in admiration
White Mason says the case is remarkable and peculiar

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: Remarkable! most remarkable! I can hardly recall any case where the features have been more peculiar.

events.label: White Mason says he has told Holmes how matters stood up to his takeover

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: I thought you would say so, Mr. Holmes. We’re well up with the times in Sussex. I’ve told you now how matters were, up to the time when I took over from Sergeant Wilson between three and four this morning. My word! I made the old mare go! But I need not have been in such a hurry, as it turned out; for there was nothing immediate that I could do. Sergeant Wilson had all the facts. I checked them and considered them and maybe added a few of my own.

events.label: Holmes asks what the examined items were

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: What were they?

events.label: A hammer is examined with Dr. Wood's help
White Mason explains his hope about the hammer

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: I was hoping that if Mr. Douglas defended himself with the hammer, he might have left his mark upon the murderer before he dropped it on the mat.

events.label: MacDonald remarks that the hammer proves nothing

communicates.speaker: macdonald
communicates.content: That, of course, proves nothing at all. There has been many a hammer murder and no trace on the hammer.

events.label: White Mason examines the gun
Sergeant Wilson points out the wired triggers

communicates.speaker: sergeant_wilson
communicates.content: They were buckshot cartridges, and the triggers were wired together so that, if you pulled on the hinder one, both barrels were discharged.

events.label: Holmes identifies the gun maker from the barrel markings

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: Pennsylvania Small Arms Company—well-known American firm.

events.label: White Mason suggests the gun is American and the killer was American

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: No doubt it is an American shotgun. I seem to have read that a sawed-off shotgun is a weapon used in some parts of America. Apart from the name upon the barrel, the idea had occurred to me. There is some evidence then, that this man who entered the house and killed its master was an American.

events.label: MacDonald rejects the claim that a stranger was in the house

communicates.speaker: macdonald
communicates.content: Man, you are surely travelling overfast. I have heard no evidence yet that any stranger was ever in the house at all. The open window, the blood on the sill, the queer card, the marks of boots in the corner, the gun! Nothing there that could not have been arranged. Mr. Douglas was an American, or had lived long in America. So had Mr. Barker. You don’t need to import an American from outside in order to account for American doings.

events.label: MacDonald asks about Ames and his reliability

communicates.speaker: macdonald
communicates.content: Ames—what about him? Is he reliable?

events.label: White Mason describes Ames's service

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: Ten years with Sir Charles Chandos—as solid as a rock. He has been with Douglas ever since he took the Manor House five years ago. He has never seen a gun of this sort in the house.

events.label: MacDonald objects that the gun could have been concealed

communicates.speaker: macdonald
communicates.content: The gun was made to conceal. That’s why the barrels were sawed. It would fit into any box. How could he swear there was no such gun in the house?

events.label: MacDonald says Ames had never seen such a gun

communicates.speaker: macdonald
communicates.content: Well, anyhow, he had never seen one.

events.label: MacDonald argues that no one entered the house

communicates.speaker: macdonald
communicates.content: I’m not convinced yet that there was ever anyone in the house. I’m asking you to conseedar what it involves if you suppose that this gun was ever brought into the house, and that all these strange things were done by a person from outside. Oh, man, it’s just inconceivable! It’s clean against common sense! I put it to you, Mr. Holmes, judging it by what we have heard.

events.label: Holmes asks White Mason to state his case

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: state your case, Mr. Mac

events.label: White Mason argues that the man was not a burglar and that the ring business and the card pointed to premeditated murder for a private reason

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: The man is not a burglar, supposing that he ever existed. The ring business and the card point to premeditated murder for some private reason.

events.label: Holmes accepts the argument

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: Very good.

events.label: White Mason presents the murder scenario and the weapon-choice argument

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: Here is a man who slips into a house with the deliberate intention of committing murder. He knows, if he knows anything, that he will have a difficulty in making his escape, as the house is surrounded with water. What weapon would he choose? You would say the most silent in the world. Then he could hope when the deed was done to slip quickly from the window, to wade the moat, and to get away at his leisure. But is it understandable that he should go out of his way to bring with him the most noisy weapon he could select, knowing well that it will fetch every human being in the house to the spot as quick as they can run, and that it is all odds that he will be seen before he can get across the moat? Is that credible, Mr. Holmes?

events.label: Holmes replies that the case is strongly put and needs justification

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: You put the case strongly. It certainly needs a good deal of justification.

events.label: Holmes asks whether the farther side of the moat was examined for signs of escape

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: May I ask, Mr. White Mason, whether you examined the farther side of the moat at once to see if there were any signs of the man having climbed out from the water?

events.label: White Mason reports that there were no signs, tracks, or marks on the farther side of the moat

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: There were no signs, Mr. Holmes. But it is a stone ledge, and one could hardly expect them. None.

events.label: Holmes asks to go down to the house at once

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: Would there be any objection, Mr. White Mason, to our going down to the house at once? There may possibly be some small point which might be suggestive.

events.label: White Mason agrees and says he wanted to put Holmes in touch with all the facts first

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: I was going to propose it, Mr. Holmes; but I thought it well to put you in touch with all the facts before we go. I suppose if anything should strike you—

events.label: Inspector MacDonald says he has worked with Holmes before

communicates.speaker: macdonald
communicates.content: I have worked with Mr. Holmes before. He plays the game.

events.label: Holmes states his view of the game and his working method

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: My own idea of the game, at any rate, is that I go into a case to help the ends of justice and the work of the police. If I have ever separated myself from the official force, it is because they have first separated themselves from me. I have no wish ever to score at their expense. At the same time, Mr. White Mason, I claim the right to work in my own way and give my results at my own time—complete rather than in stages.

events.label: White Mason welcomes Holmes and invites Watson along

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: I am sure we are honoured by your presence and to show you all we know. Come along, Dr. Watson, and when the time comes we'll all hope for a place in your book.

events.label: The group walks down the village street toward the manor house
Watson describes the manor house and its moat, garden, and drawbridge
White Mason identifies the window by the drawbridge and says it is open as it was found the previous night.

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: That’s the window, that one on the immediate right of the drawbridge. It’s open just as it was found last night.

events.label: Holmes inspects the moat edge, stone ledge, and grass border.
White Mason says there is no sign that anyone landed and asks why a sign would be left.

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: I’ve had a good look, Mr. Holmes. There is nothing there, no sign that anyone has landed—but why should he leave any sign?

events.label: Holmes asks about the water and White Mason answers that the stream brings down clay and makes it generally turbid.

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: Is the water always turbid?

events.label: Holmes asks the depth of the water and White Mason states its depth at the sides and middle.

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: How deep is it?

communicates.speaker: holmes

events.label: Holmes and the others cross the drawbridge and are admitted by the butler Ames.

White Mason asks Sergeant Wilson if there is anything fresh, then orders him home, tells Ames to wait outside, and instructs that Cecil Barker, Mrs. Douglas, and the housekeeper be warned they may be wanted.

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: Anything fresh, Sergeant Wilson? No, sir. Then you can go home. You’ve had enough. We can send for you if we want you. The butler had better wait outside. Tell him to warn Mr. Cecil Barker, Mrs. Douglas, and the housekeeper that we may want a word with them presently.

events.label: White Mason asks to give the assembled men the views he has formed first.

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: Now, gentlemen, perhaps you will allow me to give you the views I have formed first, and then you will be able to arrive at your own.

events.label: MacDonald speaks of White Mason’s professional abilities.
Holmes listens intently to White Mason.
White Mason argues that the death was not suicide and must therefore have been murder.

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: Is it suicide, or is it murder—that’s our first question, gentlemen, is it not? If it were suicide, then we have to believe that this man began by taking off his wedding ring and concealing it; that he then came down here in his dressing gown, trampled mud into a corner behind the curtain in order to give the idea someone had waited for him, opened the window, put blood on the—

events.label: White Mason supposes that the crime was done by someone inside the house and describes the sequence required.
Holmes agrees with the preceding theory discussion

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: I am inclined to agree with you.

events.label: The discussion reconstructs the intruder's entry and attack on Douglas

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: Well, now, we can reconstruct things on those lines. Mr. Douglas enters the room. He puts down the candle. A man appears from behind the curtain. He is armed with this gun. He demands the wedding ring—Heaven only knows why, but so it must have been. Mr. Douglas gave it up. Then either in cold blood or in the course of a struggle—Douglas may have gripped the hammer that was found upon the mat—he shot Douglas in this horrible way. He dropped his gun and also it would seem this queer card—V.V. 341, whatever that may mean—and he made his escape through the window and across the moat at the very moment when Cecil Barker was discovering the crime.

events.label: MacDonald objects to the proposed theory and demands a lead from Holmes

communicates.speaker: macdonald
communicates.content: Man, it would be absolute nonsense if it wasn’t that anything else is even worse! Somebody killed the man, and whoever it was I could clearly prove to you that he should have done it some other way. What does he mean by allowing his retreat to be cut off like that? What does he mean by using a shotgun when silence was his one chance of escape? Come, Mr. Holmes, it’s up to you to give us a lead, since you say Mr. White Mason’s theory is unconvincing.

events.label: Holmes kneels by the body and asks for the butler

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: I should like a few more facts before I get so far as a theory, Mr. Mac. Dear me! these injuries are really appalling. Can we have the butler in for a moment?... Ames, I understand that you have often seen this very unusual mark—a branded triangle inside a circle—upon Mr. Douglas’s forearm? You never heard any speculation as to what it meant?

events.label: Ames says that Douglas cut himself while shaving yesterday morning

communicates.speaker: ames
communicates.content: he cut himself in shaving yesterday morning

events.label: Ames says that Douglas had not cut himself in shaving for a very long time

communicates.speaker: ames
communicates.content: Not for a very long time

events.label: Ames says that Douglas was a little restless and excited yesterday

communicates.speaker: ames
communicates.content: he was a little restless and excited

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: It gives me the impression of a secret society of some sort; the same with his badge upon the forearm.

events.label: Holmes proposes a working hypothesis about the murder

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: We can adopt it as a working hypothesis and then see how far our difficulties disappear. An agent from such a society makes his way into the house, waits for Mr. Douglas, blows his head nearly off with this weapon, and escapes by wading the moat, after leaving a card beside the dead man, which will, when mentioned in the papers, tell other members of the society that vengeance has been done. But why this gun, of all weapons? And why the missing ring? And why no arrest?

events.label: Holmes examines the blood mark on the sill

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: What’s this under the side table? Dumb-bell—there’s only one. Where’s the other?

communicates.speaker: cecil_barker
communicates.content: Sorry to interrupt your consultation, but you should hear the latest news.

events.label: People inspect the found bicycle in the drive

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: Come and have a look. It is within a hundred yards of the hall door.

communicates.speaker: white_mason
communicates.content: It would be a grand help to the police if these things were numbered and registered. But we must be thankful for what we’ve got. And how in the world has he got away without it? We don’t seem to get a gleam of light in the case, Mr. Holmes.

events.label: Ames gives an account of Douglas's movements and the events after the bell rings

communicates.speaker: ames
communicates.content: He had been engaged five years before, when Douglas first came to Birlstone. He understood that Mr. Douglas was a rich gentleman who had made his money in America. He had been a kind and considerate employer. He never saw any signs of apprehension in Mr. Douglas. He ordered the drawbridge to be pulled up every night. Mr. Douglas seldom went to London or left the village; but on the day before the crime he had been shopping at Tunbridge Wells. He had observed restlessness and excitement in Mr. Douglas that day. He had not gone to bed that night; but was in the pantry putting away the silver when he heard the bell ring violently. He heard no shot. The housekeeper had come out of her room. They had gone to the front of the house together. He had seen Mrs. Douglas coming down the stairs. Mr. Barker had rushed out of the study and begged Mrs. Douglas to go back. Mrs. Douglas had gone back after persuasion. She did not scream. She made no outcry. Mrs. Allen had taken her upstairs and stayed with her in the bedroom. Ames and Mr. Barker had then returned to the study, where they had found everything exactly as the police had seen it. The candle was not lit; but the lamp was burning. They had looked out of the window, but nothing could be seen or heard. They had then rushed out into the hall, where Ames had turned the windlass which lowered the drawbridge. Mr. Barker had then hurried off to get the police.

communicates.content: No, he turned me back upon the stairs. He begged me to return to my room.

communicates.content: It may have been a couple of minutes. It is so hard to reckon time at such a moment. He implored me not to go on. He assured me that I could do nothing. Then Mrs. Allen, the housekeeper, led me upstairs again. It was all like some dreadful dream.

communicates.content: Can you give us any idea how long your husband had been downstairs before you heard the shot?

communicates.speaker: mrs_douglas
communicates.content: No, I cannot say. He went from his dressing room, and I did not hear him go. He did the round of the house every night, for he was nervous of fire. It is the only thing that I have ever known him nervous of.

events.label: The inspector asks about danger from America

communicates.speaker: macdonald
communicates.content: That is just the point which I want to come to, Mrs. Douglas. You have known your husband only in England, have you not? Have you heard him speak of anything which occurred in America and might bring some danger upon him?

events.label: Mrs. Douglas says she and her husband had been married five years and that he kept the danger from her

communicates.speaker: mrs_douglas
communicates.content: Yes, we have been married five years. Yes, I have always felt that there was a danger hanging over him. He refused to discuss it with me. It was not from want of confidence in me—there was the most complete love and confidence between us—but it was out of his desire to keep all alarm away from me. He thought I should brood over it if I knew all, and so he was silent.

events.label: Mrs. Douglas explains how she learned of her husband's secret past

communicates.speaker: mrs_douglas
communicates.content: Can a husband ever carry about a secret all his life and a woman who loves him have no suspicion of it? I knew it by his refusal to talk about some episodes in his American life. I knew it by certain precautions he took. I knew it by certain words he let fall. I knew it by the way he looked at unexpected strangers. I was perfectly certain that he had some powerful enemies, that he believed they were on his track, and that he was always on his guard against them. I was so sure of it that for years I have been terrified if ever he came home later than was expected.

communicates.speaker: holmes

communicates.speaker: mrs_douglas
communicates.content: I did; but his face would become very grave and he would shake his head. 'It is bad enough that one of us should have been in its shadow,' he said. 'Please God it shall never fall upon you!' It was some real valley in which he had lived and in which something terrible had occurred to him, of that I am certain; but I can tell you no more.

events.label: Mrs. Douglas reports that Mr. Douglas once spoke the name Bodymaster McGinty while delirious

communicates.speaker: mrs_douglas
communicates.content: Yes, he was delirious with fever once when he had his hunting accident three years ago. Then I remember that there was a name that came continually to his lips. He spoke it with anger and a sort of horror. McGinty was the name—Bodymaster McGinty. I asked him when he recovered who Bodymaster McGinty was, and whose body he was master of. 'Never of mine, thank God!' he answered with a laugh, and that was all I could get from him. But there is a connection between Bodymaster McGinty and the Valley of Fear.

events.label: Mrs. Douglas answers questions about the engagement and wedding

communicates.content: There was romance. There is always romance. There was nothing mysterious. No, I was quite free.

events.label: Mrs. Douglas responds to the question about the wedding ring

communicates.speaker: mrs_douglas

The man who tears a wedding ring off a dead man’s—What do you say to it, Mr. Holmes?

communicates.content: there’s not a doubt of it! Barker has just marked the window himself. It’s a good deal broader than any bootmark. I mind that you said it was a splay-foot, and here’s the explanation. But what’s the game, Mr. Holmes—what’s the game?

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: The whole story told by Barker is a lie. But Barker’s story is corroborated by Mrs. Douglas. Therefore she is lying also. They are both lying, and in a conspiracy. Why are they lying, and what is the truth which they are trying so hard to conceal?

events.label: Holmes argues that the ring, card, and timing in the story make the account impossible

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: the assassin had less than a minute after the murder had been committed to take that ring, which was under another ring, from the dead man’s finger, to replace the other ring and to put that singular card beside his victim; the ring could not have been taken before the man was killed; the assassin was alone with the dead man for some time with the lamp lit; the shot must have been fired some time earlier than we are told; there was a deliberate conspiracy upon the part of the two people who heard the gunshot

communicates.content: the blood mark on the windowsill was deliberately placed there by Barker, in order to give a false clue to the police

events.label: Holmes replies about Barker and Mrs. Douglas concealing the truth

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: If you put it that Mrs. Douglas and Barker know the truth about the murder, and are conspiring to conceal it, then I can give you a whole-souled answer. I am sure they do.

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: That, I am sure, cannot be true. Well, at least they gave that impression. However, we will suppose that they are an extraordinarily astute couple, who deceive everyone upon this point, and conspire to murder the husband. He happens to be a man over whose head some danger hangs— We have only their word for that.

events.label: Holmes responds thoughtfully and outlines Watson's theory

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: I see, Watson. You are sketching out a theory by which everything they say from the beginning is false. Let us see what that brings us to.

events.label: Holmes describes the couple inventing an explanation for the crime and staging evidence

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: They invent this theory to account for the crime. They then play up to the idea by leaving this bicycle in the park as proof of the existence of some outsider. The stain on the windowsill conveys the same idea. So does the card on the body, which might have been prepared in the house. That all fits into your hypothesis, Watson.

events.label: Holmes questions the shotgun, the alarm risk, and Mrs. Allen's possible inquiry

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: But now we come on the nasty, angular, uncompromising bits which won’t slip into their places. Why a cut-off shotgun of all weapons—and an American one at that? How could they be so sure that the sound of it would not bring someone on to them? It’s a mere chance as it is that Mrs. Allen did not start out to inquire for the slamming door. Why did your guilty couple do all this, Watson?

events.label: Watson says he cannot explain it

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: I confess that I can’t explain it.

events.label: Holmes challenges the probability of a guilty couple removing a wedding ring and hiding a bicycle

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: And then again, if a woman and her lover conspire to murder a husband, are they going to advertise their guilt by ostentatiously removing his wedding ring after his death? Does that strike you as very probable, Watson? And once again, if the thought of leaving a bicycle concealed outside had occurred to you, would it really have seemed worth doing when the dullest detective would naturally say this is an obvious blind, as the bicycle is the first thing which the fugitive needed in order to make his escape. I can conceive of no explanation. And yet there should be no combination of events for which the wit of man cannot conceive an explanation. Simply as a mental exercise, without any assertion that it is true, let me indicate a possible line of thought. It is, I admit, mere imagination; but how often is imagination the mother of truth?

events.label: Holmes proposes a hypothetical guilty secret, murder by an avenger, and the taking of the wedding ring

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: We will suppose that there was a guilty secret, a really shameful secret in the life of this man Douglas. This leads to his murder by someone who is, we will suppose, an avenger, someone from outside. This avenger, for some reason which I confess I am still at a loss to explain, took the dead man’s wedding ring. The vendetta might conceivably date back to the man’s first marriage, and the ring be taken for some such reason.

events.label: Holmes proposes that Barker and the wife arrive, are warned, and let the assassin go

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: Before this avenger got away, Barker and the wife had reached the room. The assassin convinced them that any attempt to arrest him would lead to the publication of some hideous scandal. They were converted to this idea, and preferred to let him go. For this purpose they probably lowered the bridge, which can be done quite noiselessly, and then raised it again.

events.label: Holmes proposes the assassin escapes on foot and leaves the bicycle concealed

communicates.speaker: holmes
communicates.content: He made his escape, and for some reason thought that he could do so more safely on foot than on the bicycle. He therefore left his machine where it would not be discovered until he had got safely away. So far we are within the bounds of possibility, are we not?

communicates.content: So little that it was evident that he had carefully guarded himself against identification. There were no papers or letters, and no marking upon the clothes. A cycle map of the county lay on his bedroom table. He had left the hotel after breakfast yesterday morning on his bicycle, and no more was heard of him until our inquiries.

events.label: MacDonald reports the man's description

communicates.speaker: macdonald
communicates.content: Here we have it so far as they could give it. They don’t seem to have taken any very particular stock of him; but still the porter, the clerk, and the chambermaid are all agreed that this about covers the points. He was a man about five foot nine in height, fifty or so years of age, his hair slightly grizzled, a grayish moustache, a curved nose, and a face which all of them described as fierce and forbidding. He was dressed in a heavy gray suit with a reefer jacket, and he wore a short yellow overcoat and a soft cap.

events.label: MacDonald describes the shotgun and how it could be carried

communicates.speaker: macdonald
communicates.content: It is less than two feet long. It could very well have fitted into his valise. He could have carried it inside his overcoat without difficulty.

events.label: MacDonald outlines his reconstruction of Hargrave's movements and murder

communicates.speaker: macdonald
communicates.content: When we have got our man, we shall be better able to judge. But, even as it stands, we have surely gone a long way. We know that an American calling himself Hargrave came to Tunbridge Wells two days ago with bicycle and valise. In the latter was a sawed-off shotgun; so he came with the deliberate purpose of crime. Yesterday morning he set off for this place on his bicycle, with his gun concealed in his overcoat. No one saw him arrive, so far as we can learn; but he need not pass through the village to reach the park gates, and there are many cyclists upon the road. Presumably he at once concealed his cycle among the laurels where it was found, and possibly lurked there himself, with his eye on the house, waiting for Mr. Douglas to come out. The shotgun is a strange weapon to use inside a house; but he had intended to use it outside, and there it has very obvious advantages, as it would be impossible to miss with it, and the sound of shots is so common in an English sporting neighbourhood that no particular notice would be taken. Mr. Douglas did not appear. He left his bicycle and approached the house in the twilight. He found the bridge down and no one about. He took his chance, intending, no doubt, to make some excuse if he met anyone. He met no one. He slipped into the first room that he saw, and concealed himself behind the curtain. Thence he could see the drawbridge go up, and he knew that his only escape was through the moat. He waited until quarter-past eleven, when Mr. Douglas upon his usual nightly round came into the room. He shot him and escaped, as arranged. He was aware that the bicycle would be described by the hotel people and be a clue against him; so he left it there and made his way by some other means to London or to some safe hiding place which he had already arranged.
